summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national framework. Identity-document rules, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules governing places of deprivation of liberty apply here as French law, and the French prison framework binds the island's establishments as French prisons.

Nothing in that framework criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage is lawful on the island, which has been part of France since the 1975 vote to remain within the Republic; it is one of few jurisdictions in Africa and in the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed. The National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people is French law and therefore applies on Mayotte.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document rather than anatomy, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Reporting from January 2018 found that trans women are consequently held in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them.

The independent body that inspects French places of deprivation of liberty, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all such establishments. Its finding rests on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. As French establishments, the island's jails stand under that same oversight and that same record.

Formal entitlement does not map smoothly onto daily life. A Mayotte university-centre teacher and his Malagasy partner, married at Sada Town Hall in a process described as long and complicated, illustrate the distance between the rights written in French law and what couples actually encounter on this predominantly Muslim island.

Counsel specialised in these questions is scarce locally. A directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while a Paris-based lawyer listed at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation is offered as available to those needing advice on persons and family law.
tangentialFactors:
Mayotte's position creates a split between the law on the books and the law in practice. The statutory regime is identical to metropolitan France's, yet local reporting describes administrative paths for couples and for gender recognition as drawn out, which raises the practical cost of exercising rights that are formally unconditional.

The island's predominantly Muslim social environment shapes how those rights are received. Same-sex marriage being available here places Mayotte alongside a small number of jurisdictions in Africa and the Muslim-majority world, an outlier status that cuts both ways: the ceremony can lawfully take place at a town hall, and the couple going there may attract attention that a couple in mainland France would not.

Conditions of confinement are governed by national practice rather than local policy. The CGLPL's 2021 findings about violations affecting transgender detainees derive from mainland inspections, so they describe the framework Mayotte's establishments are bound by; no source in this inventory reports an inspection or a documented incident at a Mayotte facility itself.

Access to representation is thinner than the statutory rights suggest. With no referenced local lawyer in the relevant directories, anyone on the island needing counsel on identity documents, family status or discrimination is pointed toward Paris, which implies travel, cost and delay.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mayotte use the same civil-status procedure as the rest of France to change their legal gender, following the simplification voted by the National Assembly. The application is filed through the local civil registry under French rules.

Marriage between two men or two women can be celebrated at Mayotte's town halls, as at Sada, without any territorial exception to the national marriage regime. Couples who do so report navigating a demanding administrative sequence before the ceremony takes place.

Anyone detained on the island is placed according to the gender marker on their identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women held under that rule are typically accommodated in all-male facilities, where the 2018 reporting recorded threats from other detainees; the CGLPL receives referrals about conditions for transgender detainees and can inspect French places of deprivation of liberty, including local jails.

Legal aid locally is limited in specialist terms. Directories listing LGBT-friendly lawyers return no entry for Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada or other Mayotte towns, so residents seeking counsel on status, family or discrimination matters generally deal with practitioners based in Paris.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Mayotte's own places of detention currently hold a trans detainee, and under what conditions, is not sourced here. The evidence in this inventory about treatment in custody is national: the CGLPL's May 2021 opinion reports referrals since 2010 and interviews conducted at four mainland establishments, none of them on Mayotte.

The 2021 CGLPL opinion does not state what proportion of the roughly forty transgender people behind its referrals were held on overseas departments rather than the mainland; attributing any specific number of violations to Mayotte would therefore go beyond the sources.

No source in this inventory reports a hate-crime conviction, a discrimination complaint or a refusal of service involving a trans person on Mayotte. The anti-discrimination statute is asserted as applicable because it is French law, but its enforcement on the island is not documented here.

Local legal-access figures come from a single directory's empty results for Mayotte towns. That directory may be incomplete rather than exhaustive, so the claim that no LGBT-friendly lawyer practises on the island is best read as an absence of listed providers rather than a proven absence of practitioners.

How quickly the simplified gender-recognition procedure has been processed by Mayotte's civil registry since the National Assembly vote is not stated in the available sources.
